summary: Specifies an automatic tunneling mechanism that lets a service provider deliver IPv6 to customers over its IPv4 network. It uses stateless operation, automatic prefix delegation and simple provisioning. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending the new kind of internet mail through the old kind of roads by wrapping it in an envelope the old roads understand.

questions: ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling for isps
how does 6rd build an ipv6 prefix
subtitle: How an ISP can hand customers native-looking IPv6 over its existing IPv4 network, with no tunnel state to keep.

tldr.problem: Service providers wanted to give customers IPv6 quickly, but their access networks only carried IPv4 and they wanted to change as little of it as possible.
tldr.mechanism: Customer routers build their IPv6 prefix by combining the provider's 6rd prefix with all or part of their own IPv4 address, then tunnel IPv6 inside IPv4 to other customers or to a Border Relay. The IPv4 address embedded in each IPv6 address tells the sender where the tunnel ends.
tldr.outcome: Customers get IPv6 service equivalent to native IPv6 while the provider keeps running IPv4 unchanged, and 6rd may be discontinued once the network supports native IPv6.

today: RFC 5969 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The text itself says 6rd may be discontinued once the provider network supports fully native IPv6.

sections.title: What 6rd Is
sections.content:
6rd is a protocol mechanism for delivering IPv6 to customer sites across a service provider's (SP's) IPv4 network. It builds on 6to4 (RFC 3056) but, instead of the well-known prefix 2002::/16, it uses the SP's own IPv6 prefix. That keeps the operational domain of 6rd inside the SP network, under the SP's control. To customer sites and the wider IPv6 Internet, the service looks equivalent to native IPv6.

The mechanism relies on an algorithmic mapping between the IPv6 and IPv4 addresses used in the SP network. That lets a router work out the IPv4 tunnel endpoint from an IPv6 prefix, so operation is stateless. The original idea and name come from RFC 5569.

A 6rd domain consists of 6rd Customer Edge (CE) routers and one or more 6rd Border Relays (BRs). Encapsulated IPv6 packets follow the IPv4 routing topology between CEs and BRs, and a BR is traversed only for IPv6 traffic to or from outside the domain. 6rd could be seen as a superset of 6to4: setting the 6rd prefix to 2002::/16 would give 6to4.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet company wraps new-style packets in old-style envelopes. Houses and a few special gateways know how to unwrap them.

sections.title: How the Delegated Prefix Is Built
sections.content:
A CE creates its 6rd delegated prefix by concatenating the 6rd prefix (n bits) and a consecutive run of bits from its own IPv4 address (o bits). The result is used like a prefix from DHCPv6 prefix delegation. The remaining bits split into a subnet ID and an interface ID. To allow stateless address autoconfiguration on the LAN side, the delegated prefix SHOULD be /64 or shorter.

Example from the RFC: with a /32 6rd prefix and 24 bits of the IPv4 address (all CE addresses fall inside 10.0.0.0/8), each CE gets a /56, because 32 + 24 = 56.

Embedding fewer than 32 bits is possible only when the IPv4 addresses are aggregated, which is quite likely with private addresses. Each 6rd domain may encode the IPv4 address differently and has its own 6rd prefix.

Because the prefix is derived from the IPv4 address, changing that address changes the IPv6 prefix, which could be disruptive, so the SP is advised to give CEs long address lifetimes. Prefix lifetimes advertised on the LAN side MUST be equal to or shorter than the IPv4 lease time.
sections.plainLanguage: Your new-style address is your provider's street name plus the number of your old-style address. So the provider can always work out one from the other.

sections.title: Configuration and the DHCPv4 Option
sections.content:
Every CE and BR in a domain MUST be configured with four values, identical across the domain: IPv4MaskLen (the number of high-order bits shared by all CE IPv4 addresses), 6rdPrefix, 6rdPrefixLen and 6rdBRIPv4Address. The CE needs only its own IPv4 address on top of these to compute its delegated prefix.

The RFC defines one way to deliver them: a DHCPv4 option, OPTION_6RD (code 212). A CE that configures IPv4 by DHCP SHOULD implement it. The option carries IPv4MaskLen, 6rdPrefixLen, a 16-octet 6rdPrefix and one or more BR IPv4 addresses. IPv4MaskLen may be 0 to 32, and (32 - IPv4MaskLen) + 6rdPrefixLen MUST be at most 128. The option length is 22 octets with one BR address. The CE MUST include it in its Parameter Request List, and MUST be able to disable 6rd, in which case a received option is silently ignored.

Since DHCP cannot convey more than one instance of an option, the option provisions at most one 6rd domain. When enabled, a typical CE installs a default route toward the BR, a null route for its delegated prefix, and routes for LAN prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the neighborhood is told the same four facts, such as the street name and where the gateway is. After that each house can work out its own address.

sections.title: Encapsulation, MTU and Receiving Rules
sections.content:
IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation follows Section 3.5 of RFC 4213, the same as 6to4. By default the IPv6 Traffic Class MUST be copied to the IPv4 ToS field, though configuration may override this. The 6rd link is modeled as an NBMA link, with all CEs and BRs as off-link neighbors of each other.

For MTU, if the SP's IPv4 MTU is well managed, the tunnel MTU should be the IPv4 MTU minus the 20-byte encapsulating header, for example 1480 bytes for a 1500-byte IPv4 MTU. Absent better information, the 6rd Tunnel MTU SHOULD default to 1280 bytes. A BR using an anycast source address MUST set the IPv4 Don't Fragment flag, because fragments from different BRs with the same fragment ID could be reassembled incorrectly.

To prevent spoofing, a BR or CE MUST check that the IPv4 source address embedded in the encapsulated IPv6 source matches the outer IPv4 source. If they differ, the packet MUST be dropped and a counter incremented. A CE must still allow packets sourced by the configured BR address, and by default MUST drop packets from the 6rd virtual interface for IPv6 destinations outside its own delegated prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope adds a little weight, so the parcel inside has to be a bit smaller. Every gateway also checks that the return address on the envelope matches the one inside, to catch cheaters.

sections.title: Border Relays, Anycast and Reachability
sections.content:
A BR sits at the edge of a 6rd domain with an IPv4 interface, a 6rd virtual interface and an IPv6 interface to the native network. Because 6rd is stateless, the BR's IPv4 address may be an anycast address shared across the domain for reliability and load balancing, and any BR may be used at any time. If so, the relay MUST use that anycast address as the source address of packets it relays to CEs, and the address must be advertised in the SP's IGP. No specific routes need to be advertised externally in IPv6 or IPv4 BGP.

Sending Neighbor Unreachability Detection or other periodic packets between CEs beyond isolated troubleshooting is NOT RECOMMENDED, and periodic NUD to a BR from very many CEs could overload it. A CE that needs to check BR reachability MUST use a method that follows the normal data path. The RFC describes one: the CE sends an IPv6 packet whose source and destination are both addresses in its own delegated prefix, wrapped in IPv4 addressed to the BR. The BR decapsulates and forwards it normally back to the CE, completing a round trip without special processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Many identical gateways can share one address, and any of them can do the job. To check a gateway works, mail yourself a letter through it.

sections.title: Security and Address Space
sections.content:
Limiting 6rd to one provider network means a CE needs to accept packets only from one or a few known BR IPv4 addresses, so many of the 6to4 threats described in RFC 3964 do not apply. With the receiving rules of Section 9.2, IPv6 packets are as well protected against spoofing as IPv4 packets inside an SP network.

The RFC does describe a forwarding-loop risk: a malicious user who knows the BR address could craft packets that make a BR reflect tunneled traffic out of the domain, and loops between 6rd domains could allow a packet amplification attack. Mitigations include making the BR IPv4 address unreachable from outside the domain, filtering tunneled packets sourced from it, and filtering known relay addresses. The BR MUST install a null route for its own delegated prefix, except for the IPv6 Subnet-Router anycast address.

On address space, 6rd uses ordinary provider allocations, so no global block like 2002::/16 is needed. In the worst case, with all 32 IPv4 bits embedded and a /56 per site, a provider needs a /24; if the IPv4 addresses are aggregated, fewer bits are used. With non-aggregatable IPv4 space, the 6rd prefix MUST be no longer than /32 to offer at least a /64.
sections.plainLanguage: Because only one company runs the whole system, the gateway knows who is allowed to send parcels. A few tricky tricks could still make parcels bounce around, so the RFC lists ways to stop them.

sections.title: Moving to Native IPv6
sections.content: The SP can migrate to IPv6 at its own pace with little or no effect on customers using 6rd, and an administrator can disable 6rd when native IPv6 is available. If a separate address block is used for native service, the move is a normal renumbering event for the customer. Renumbering may be avoided by injecting the 6rd delegated prefix into the SP's IPv6 routing domain. The 6rd block can be reclaimed once all users have moved to native service. The RFC leaves further transition details out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When the new roads are finally built, the provider can stop using the envelopes. Customers may need new addresses unless the provider plans to avoid that.
